desc:
You are given an array nums of positive integers and a list of queries [l, r]. For a query, look only at the subarray nums[l..r] (both ends included) and decide whether it can be cut at one place into two non-empty parts, a left part and a right part, with equal sums.

Return an array with one entry per query, in order: 1 if such a cut exists and 0 otherwise. A subarray with a single element can never be cut.

nums = [2, 1, 1, 4, 3, 5]
[0, 2] -> 1   ([2] | [1, 1])
[1, 3] -> 0   (total 6, but prefixes 1, 2, 6 never reach 3)
[0, 5] -> 1   ([2,1,1,4] | [3,5], both 8)
[3, 3] -> 0
result = [1, 0, 1, 0]
hints: For one query you could try every cut and compare the two sums, but that is O(length) per query. What must be true about the total of the subarray?
With prefix sums pre, the subarray total is pre[r+1] - pre[l]. A balanced cut has a left part summing to exactly half of that, so the total must be even.

All values are positive, so the prefix sums are strictly increasing and every value occurs at most once. Look up the wanted prefix value pre[l] + total/2 in a dictionary that maps prefix value to index; any hit lies strictly inside the range automatically.
editorial: Build the prefix array pre with pre[0] = 0. For a query [l, r] the sum is total = pre[r+1] - pre[l]. If total is odd there is no equal split. Otherwise a cut after index m (with l ≤ m < r) works exactly when pre[m+1] = pre[l] + total/2.

Because every element is positive, the prefix sums strictly increase. So each value is attained at most once and we can store them in a dictionary for O(1) lookup. If the wanted value is present, it is strictly greater than pre[l] and strictly smaller than pre[r+1] (since total > 0 whenever the range is non-empty), so it corresponds to a valid non-empty split. For a single element total/2 is positive and smaller than the element, so no prefix value matches, which agrees with the rule.
Preprocessing is O(n) and each query O(1): O(n + q) overall. If zeros or negatives were allowed, the lookup would need the first/last occurrence of each value and a binary search on the positions.
